about: Chapter 9, Coconut Farm: 69 patterns, four for each of the 15 skills (1 and 2 marks), three 3-mark and three 5-mark long answers in steps (#208), and three 4-mark case studies, drawn from the chapter's 500 questions. All DRAFT until Ashalatha approves them.

patterns.text: Given {r.a} × {r.b} = {r.p}, which related division fact is correct?

wrong.mistake: reverses the dividend and the divisor
writes the product again as the quotient
divides the two factors instead of dividing the product

patterns.hint: A division fact undoes the multiplication: the product is divided by one factor to give the other.
patterns.explanation: {r.p} ÷ {r.y} = {r.x}, because {r.y} × {r.x} = {r.p}.
patterns.misconception: Reverses the dividend and divisor or treats multiplication and division as unrelated facts.
patterns.notes: Factors 3 to 9 and 4 to 15 (different); the right fact divides by either factor, at random.

patterns.text: Use {a} × {b} = {a * b} to find {a * b} ÷ {b}.
patterns.hint: Which number times {b} makes {a * b}?
patterns.misconception: Reverses the dividend and divisor or treats multiplication and division as unrelated facts.
patterns.notes: Factors 3 to 9 and 6 to 15, different.

patterns.text: In {d * q} ÷ {d} = {q}, which number is the {role.w}?
patterns.answer: d * q if role.k == 0 else (d if role.k == 1 else q)
patterns.hint: The dividend is the number being divided, the divisor is the number you divide by, and the quotient is the answer.
patterns.explanation: In {d * q} ÷ {d} = {q}, the dividend is {d * q}, the divisor is {d} and the quotient is {q}. So the {role.w} is {d * q if role.k == 0 else (d if role.k == 1 else q)}.
patterns.misconception: Reverses the dividend and divisor or treats multiplication and division as unrelated facts.
patterns.notes: Divisor 3 to 9, quotient 6 to 16 (different); asks for the dividend, divisor or quotient at random.

patterns.text: Use {a} × {b} = {a * b} to fill both blanks: {a * b} ÷ ___ = {a} and ___ ÷ {a} = {b}. Give the first blank, then the second.

steps.text: First blank: {b}, because {a * b} ÷ {b} = {a}.
Second blank: {a * b}, because {a} × {b} = {a * b}, so {a * b} ÷ {a} = {b}.

patterns.hint: The three numbers in the family are {a}, {b} and {a * b}.
patterns.explanation: {a} × {b} = {a * b} gives {a * b} ÷ {b} = {a} and {a * b} ÷ {a} = {b}.
patterns.misconception: Reverses the dividend and divisor or treats multiplication and division as unrelated facts.
patterns.notes: Factors 4 to 9 and 11 to 19.

patterns.hint: Dividing by {d} moves each digit {'one place' if d == 10 else 'two places'} to the right.
patterns.misconception: Cancels visible zeroes without checking place value or changes only one number when using an equivalent division.

patterns.text: If {b * q * (1 if k == 0 else 10)} ÷ {b} = {q * (1 if k == 0 else 10)}, find {b * q * 10} ÷ {b * (1 if k == 0 else 10)}.
patterns.hint: {'The dividend is ten times bigger and the divisor is the same.' if k == 0 else 'The dividend is the same and the divisor is ten times bigger.'}
patterns.explanation: {'Ten times the dividend gives ten times the quotient' if k == 0 else 'Ten times the divisor gives a tenth of the quotient'}: {b * q * 10} ÷ {b * (1 if k == 0 else 10)} = {q * 10 if k == 0 else q}.

patterns.notes: Divisor 2 to 9, quotient 2 to 12; either the dividend or the divisor is made ten times bigger.

patterns.misconception: Cancels visible zeroes without checking place value or changes only one number when using an equivalent division.
patterns.notes: Divisor 200 to 900, quotient 11 to 19.

makes only the divisor ten times bigger
adds the same number to both instead of multiplying both

patterns.hint: Multiplying both numbers by the same amount keeps the quotient the same.

patterns.text: A number divided by {d} gives quotient {q} and remainder {r}. What is the number? Show the multiplication and the addition in your working.

steps.text: Multiplies: {d} × {q} = {d * q}.
Adds the remainder: {d * q} + {r} = {d * q + r}.

patterns.hint: Dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder.
patterns.misconception: Uses addition or subtraction instead of the inverse operation or places the missing value in the wrong role.
patterns.notes: Divisor 4 to 9, quotient 12 to 40, remainder 1 up to one less than the divisor.

slips by one group
uses subtraction instead of division

patterns.hint: Work out each side. Which one balances?
patterns.explanation: {r.p} ÷ {r.d} = {r.q}, because {r.d} × {r.q} = {r.p}. The others don't balance.
patterns.misconception: Uses addition or subtraction instead of the inverse operation or places the missing value in the wrong role.

patterns.text: Use splitting: {d * (qa + qb):num} ÷ {d} = ({d * qa:num} ÷ {d}) + ({d * qb} ÷ {d}). Find the quotient.
patterns.hint: Find each part: {d * qa:num} ÷ {d} and {d * qb} ÷ {d}. Then add.
patterns.explanation: {d * qa:num} ÷ {d} = {qa} and {d * qb} ÷ {d} = {qb}. {qa} + {qb} = {qa + qb}.
patterns.misconception: Splits into parts that are not divisible or forgets to combine every partial quotient.
patterns.notes: Divisor 3 to 9; the first part gives a whole number of tens (60 to 190), the second 2 to 19.

patterns.text: {d * (qa + qb):num} ÷ {d} = {qa + qb}. {d * qa:num} is split off first, giving the partial quotient {qa}. What is the other partial quotient?
patterns.hint: What is left after {d * qa:num}? Divide that by {d}.
patterns.explanation: {d * (qa + qb):num} − {d * qa:num} = {d * qb}, and {d * qb} ÷ {d} = {qb}. Check: {qa} + {qb} = {qa + qb}.
patterns.misconception: Splits into parts that are not divisible or forgets to combine every partial quotient.
patterns.notes: Divisor 3 to 9; first partial quotient 60 to 190 (tens), the other 2 to 19.

patterns.text: Which split of {r.n:num} ÷ {r.d} uses two parts that add up to {r.n:num} and that {r.d} divides exactly?

wrong.mistake: splits into parts that are not divisible by the divisor
uses parts that do not add up to the dividend
splits into parts that are not divisible by the divisor

patterns.hint: Both parts must add up to {r.n}, and {r.d} must divide each part exactly.
patterns.explanation: {r.a} + {r.b} = {r.n}, and {r.a} ÷ {r.d} = {r.qa}, {r.b} ÷ {r.d} = {r.qb}. So {r.n} ÷ {r.d} = {r.qa} + {r.qb} = {r.qa + r.qb}.
patterns.misconception: Splits into parts that are not divisible or forgets to combine every partial quotient.
patterns.notes: Divisor 3 to 9; quotient parts 60 to 180 and 3 to 17. Each wrong split fails one rule: two use parts the divisor does not divide, one uses parts that do not add up to the dividend.

patterns.text: Given {d * q:num} ÷ {d} = {q}, find {d * (q + k):num} ÷ {d} without dividing from the beginning. Show your working.

steps.text: Splits: {d * (q + k):num} = {d * q:num} + {d * k}.
{d * k} ÷ {d} = {k}, so the quotient is {q} + {k} = {q + k}.

patterns.hint: How much more than {d * q:num} is {d * (q + k):num}?
patterns.explanation: {d * (q + k):num} is {d * k} more than {d * q:num}. {d * k} ÷ {d} = {k}, so the quotient is {q + k}.
patterns.misconception: Splits into parts that are not divisible or forgets to combine every partial quotient.
patterns.notes: Divisor 3 to 9, known quotient 112 to 199, then 2 to 9 more groups.
